events.detail: In-place marking using first row and first column · claims O(m * n) time

data.approach: In-place marking using first row and first column
data.key_insight: We can use the first row and the first column of the matrix itself as markers to remember which rows and columns need to be set to zero, saving extra space. A separate boolean variable is needed to track whether the first column itself should be zeroed.

steps.title: Initialize markers
steps.detail: Check if the first row and first column have any zeros and record the state of the first column using a boolean variable.

steps.title: Mark zeros
steps.detail: Iterate through the rest of the matrix. If an element is zero, set the corresponding cell in the first row and first column to zero.

steps.title: Update matrix body
steps.detail: Iterate through the matrix starting from row 1 and column 1. Use the marks in the first row and first column to set elements to zero.

steps.title: Update first row and column
steps.detail: Finally, update the first row and first column based on the initial checks.

data.generator_code:
import random
def generate(rng, n):
    m = max(1, n)
    matrix = [[rng.randint(-10, 10) for _ in range(m)] for _ in range(m)]
    return [matrix]
def generate_worst(rng, n):
    m = max(1, n)
    matrix = [[0 if (i + j) % 2 == 0 else 1 for j in range(m)] for i in range(m)]
    return [matrix]

events.label: Coach: pattern, brute force and its bottleneck
events.detail: Pattern: Matrix Traversal with State Tracking · 3 hints

data.pattern_summary: Scanning a 2D grid while recording coordinates of interest to apply updates without cascading unwanted changes.

pattern_options.name: Matrix Traversal with State Tracking
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We need to scan the matrix to find zeros and track which rows and columns must be zeroed out.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers are used for linear sequences like arrays or strings, not 2D grid propagation.

pattern_options.name: Sliding window
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Sliding windows track subarrays or subgrids of fixed sizes, not individual row and column zeros.

pattern_options.name: Breadth-First Search
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. BFS explores neighbors level by level in graphs, whereas this problem requires updating entire rows and columns based on a condition.

signals.hint: Implies you must update the existing data structure rather than returning a new one.

signals.phrase: set its entire row and column to 0
signals.hint: Indicates that finding a zero triggers updates across multiple other cells in the grid.

data.brute_force_idea: Make a complete copy of the matrix. Iterate through every cell in the copy, and whenever you find a 0, update the corresponding row and column in the original matrix.
data.brute_force_why: We visit every element in an m by n matrix, and for each zero found, we iterate through its entire row and column of length m and n.
data.bottleneck: Creating a full deep copy of the matrix takes extra space and time.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how much memory is being duplicated at the start.
Can you remember which rows and columns need to be zeroed without duplicating the entire matrix?
Consider storing your markers directly inside the matrix itself.

Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.overview: Set Matrix Zeroes modifies an in-place 2D matrix so that if any cell contains zero, its entire row and column become zero. It achieves O(1) extra space by repurposing the matrix's own first row and column as marker storage.
data.intuition: Think of the first row and column as scoreboard trackers at the edge of a game board. They record which rows and columns have scored a zero, leaving the inner cells free to be updated later.

flow_nodes.detail: Gets matrix size and sets is_first_col_zero to false.

flow_nodes.label: Mark rows and columns
flow_nodes.detail: Iterates through the matrix to set markers in the first row and column.

flow_nodes.label: Zero inner matrix
flow_nodes.detail: Uses the markers to update inner cells to zero.

flow_nodes.label: Zero first row?
flow_nodes.detail: Checks if the top-left cell requires zeroing the first row.

flow_nodes.detail: Checks if the saved flag requires zeroing the first column.

flow_nodes.detail: The matrix has been completely modified in place.

pitfalls: Forgetting to track the first column state independently using a boolean variable.
Updating the first row and column markers prematurely before scanning the inner matrix.
Confusing matrix boundary indices leading to out-of-bounds errors.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: Instead of allocating an extra matrix to remember which rows and columns need to be zeroed, the optimized solution uses the matrix's own first row and first column as storage flags. A separate boolean variable tracks whether the first column itself needs to be zeroed to prevent indexing conflicts.

derivation.note: Loops through every row in the matrix.
Scans all inner elements of the matrix to locate zeros and update markers.
Loops through rows starting from index 1.
Iterates through inner cells to apply zero updates based on the first row and column markers.
Clears the first row if the top-left marker indicates it is required.
Clears the first column if the separate tracking flag was set.

data.time_summary: Lines 10 and 16 dominate execution, running proportional to m * n operations. All other loops run at most m or n times. Thus, the total time complexity is O(m * n).
data.space_summary: No additional data structures scaling with the input size are allocated. Only a few primitive variables are used, resulting in O(1) auxiliary space.
data.takeaway: When an algorithm requires extra memory to track state across indices of a matrix or array, check if unused parts of the input data structure can be repurposed as in-place storage flags.
mistakes: Failing to use a separate boolean flag for the first column, leading to ambiguity between the first row's marker at matrix[0][0] and the first column's marker.
Modifying the first row or first column too early in the traversal, which corrupts marker states before other elements are checked.
Forgetting to process the first row and first column separately at the very end after the inner matrix updates are complete.
